title: Digits and remainders
objectives: Find last digits and test divisibility with modular arithmetic.

screens.title: Powers of 7
screens.prose: We want the last digit of $7^{2026}$, far too long to write out. Only last digits matter: multiply the last digit by 7 and keep its last digit. Extend the table.

state.caption: The last digit of 7 times each digit.

screens.question: Fill in the last digits of $7^4$ to $7^8$.

hints.text: The last digit of $7^4$ is the last digit of $3 \times 7$.
$3 \times 7 = 21$, so $7^4$ ends in 1. Then $1 \times 7$ ends in 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the last digit above by 7 and keep only its last digit.

explain.text: Each last digit is 7 times the one above, cut to its last digit. After 1 comes 7 again, so the digits repeat 7, 9, 3, 1. The cycle has length 4.

screens.title: The power 2026
screens.prose: The cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 has length 4. So only the remainder of the power on division by 4 matters.
screens.question: What is the last digit of $7^{2026}$?

hints.text: Remainder 2 lands on the second digit of the cycle.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find 2026 modulo 4, then read that place in the cycle.

byKey.even: 2026 is even, but the cycle has length 4, not 2. The remainder on division by 4 is 2.
byKey.three: 2026 leaves 2 on division by 4, not 3. Check $4 \cdot 506 = 2024$.
byKey.seven: Remainder 1 gives 7. 2026 leaves 2, so read the second place.

explain.text: $2026 = 4 \cdot 506 + 2$, so $7^{2026}$ ends like $7^2 = 49$. Its last digit is 9. Principle: find the cycle, then reduce the power by its length.

screens.title: Tests for 9 and 11
screens.prose: The digits of 123456789 sum to 45, a multiple of 9, so 9 divides it. For 11, alternate the signs from the right.

state.caption: Signs alternate from the right, starting with + on the last digit.

screens.question: What remainder does 123456789 leave on division by 11?

hints.text: Add the digits with the signs shown.
The pairs give $1 + 1 + 1 + 1$, then add the last 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the alternating sum, not the plain digit sum.

byKey.sum: You reduced the plain digit sum, 45, modulo 11. That test is for 9; 11 needs alternating signs.
byKey.nine: 9 divides it, but 11 is a different test. Alternate the signs.

explain.text: The alternating sum is $9 - 8 + 7 - 6 + 5 - 4 + 3 - 2 + 1 = 5$. So 123456789 leaves 5 on division by 11. Principle: 10 leaves 1 modulo 9 and −1 modulo 11.

screens.title: Counting fives
screens.prose: $60! = 1 \times 2 \times \cdots \times 60$. Each trailing zero needs a 10, which is $2 \times 5$. Even numbers supply far more 2s than 5s.
screens.question: Tap every number from 1 to 60 that has a factor of 5.

hints.text: A factor of 5 means a multiple of 5.
They sit in the fifth and tenth columns.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the multiples of 5 and nothing else.

explain.text: The multiples of 5 up to 60 are the twelve numbers in the fifth and tenth columns. Each gives at least one factor of 5. The even numbers supply the 2s.

screens.title: Zeros at the end
screens.prose: You found twelve multiples of 5 up to 60. Now count the zeros at the end of $60!$.
screens.question: How many zeros end $60!$?

options.why: You counted each multiple of 5 once. 25 and 50 are $5^2$ times something, so each gives a second 5.
You counted the multiples of 10. A 5 also pairs with a spare 2 from any even number.

hints.text: Some numbers hold more than one 5.
Twelve 5s, plus one extra each from 25 and 50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every factor of 5, not every multiple.

byKey.12: Twelve multiples, but 25 and 50 each hold two 5s. That makes 14.
byKey.6: Not only the 10s count: 15 brings a 5 and 12 brings the 2 it needs.

explain.text: The twelve multiples of 5 give twelve 5s, and 25 and 50 add one more each. There are far more 2s, so each 5 makes a 10: 14 zeros. Principle: count factors, not multiples, so add $\lfloor n/25 \rfloor$.

screens.title: Work with the remainder
screens.prose: You kept only what the question needed. Last digits: work modulo 10 and use the cycle. Nine and eleven: digit sums and alternating sums. Trailing zeros: count the 5s, $$Z(n) = \left\lfloor \tfrac{n}{5} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \tfrac{n}{25} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \tfrac{n}{125} \right\rfloor + \cdots$$ This goes past Contest Practice, lesson 5 (modulo), where remainders kept big numbers small.
screens.question: How many zeros end $30!$?

byKey.once: You forgot that 25 holds a second 5.
byKey.tens: You counted only 10, 20 and 30. Every multiple of 5 brings a 5.

explain.text: $\lfloor 30/5 \rfloor + \lfloor 30/25 \rfloor = 6 + 1 = 7$. The term for 125 is 0, so we stop. Principle: each power of 5 adds its own layer.

screens.title: Why the 11 test works
screens.prose: Prove the alternating-sum test for 11. Write $d_0$ for the last digit, $d_1$ for the tens digit, and so on. Two lines may swap, and one does not belong.
screens.question: Order the proof.

lines.text: So the number $\equiv d_0 - d_1 + d_2 - \cdots \pmod{11}$.

lines.why: That holds modulo 9, not 11. Modulo 11, 10 leaves −1.

hints.text: What does 10 leave on division by 11?
It leaves −1, so its powers alternate +1 and −1.
Write the number by place value, swap each $10^k$ for $\pm 1$, then apply it.

feedback.correct: Place value, $10 \equiv -1$, the alternating sum, then the example.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both facts come before the conclusion.

byKey.d1: $10 \equiv 1$ is the fact behind the 9 test. Modulo 11, $10 \equiv -1$.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one with $10 \equiv 1$ belongs.

explain.text: Each $10^k$ leaves $(-1)^k$ on division by 11, so the digits count with alternating signs. The same proof with $10 \equiv 1$ gives the digit-sum test for 9. Principle: a divisibility test is a remainder of 10 in disguise.

screens.title: Drill: powers of 3
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. The last digits of the powers of 3 run 3, 9, 7, 1, then repeat.
screens.question: What is the last digit of $3^{2027}$?

byKey.first: Remainder 1 gives 3. 2027 leaves 3, so read the third place.

explain.text: $2027 = 4 \cdot 506 + 3$, so $3^{2027}$ ends like $3^3 = 27$. Its last digit is 7. Principle: power modulo cycle length, then read the cycle.

screens.title: Drill: a bigger factorial
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. $125!$ is the product of 1 to 125.
screens.question: How many zeros end $125!$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the 5s at every layer: 5, 25 and 125.

byKey.once: You counted multiples of 5 once each. The 25s and 125 hold more.
byKey.two: You stopped at 25. 125 is $5^3$, so it gives a third 5.

explain.text: $\lfloor 125/5 \rfloor + \lfloor 125/25 \rfloor + \lfloor 125/125 \rfloor = 25 + 5 + 1 = 31$. Principle: keep adding layers until the power of 5 passes $n$.

screens.title: Drill: a row of ones
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Look at the numbers 1, 11, 111, 1111 and so on, written only with 1s.
screens.question: How many digits has the shortest one that 7 divides?

hints.text: Track the remainder modulo 7: each step is $10r + 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the remainder modulo 7 one digit at a time.

byKey.seven: You guessed seven ones for 7. The remainder hits 0 one step earlier.
byKey.never: One does exist. The remainders must repeat, and here they reach 0 at six digits.

explain.text: The remainders modulo 7 run 1, 4, 6, 5, 2, 0. So 111111 is the first, and $111111 = 7 \times 15873$. Principle: carry only the remainder as the number grows.

screens.title: The last two digits
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer asks for the last two digits of $2^{20}$. Work modulo 100. A desk uses the same remainders: Contest Practice, lesson 5, built a checksum of trade ids this way.
screens.question: What are the last two digits of $2^{20}$? Write them as a number.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the last two digits of $2^{10}$.

byKey.double: You doubled 24. Doubling the power squares the number.

explain.text: $2^{10} = 1024$ ends in 24, and $2^{20} = (2^{10})^2$. So $2^{20}$ ends like $24^2 = 576$, in 76. Principle: square the remainder, not the number.

screens.title: Zeros in binary
screens.prose: Follow-up. Now write $60!$ in base 2. In base 2, each zero at the end is a factor of 2.
screens.question: How many zeros end $60!$ written in binary?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every factor of 2, layer by layer.

byKey.once: 30 counts each even number once. Multiples of 4, 8, 16 and 32 hold more 2s.
byKey.decimal: 14 is the count in base 10. Base 2 counts the 2s, not the 5s.

explain.text: The factors of 2 in $60!$ are $30 + 15 + 7 + 3 + 1 = 56$. Each one is a binary zero at the end. Principle: the same layered count works for any prime base.

ideas: Last digits live modulo 10: find the cycle of the powers and reduce the power by its length.
Modulo 9 a number is its digit sum; modulo 11 it is its alternating sum from the right.
Trailing zeros of $n!$ count the factors of 5, layer by layer.

formula.name: Trailing zeros
formula.note: Use 2, 4, 8 and so on for zeros in base 2.

summary.trap: $60!$ ends in 14 zeros, not 12: 25 and 50 each bring a second 5.

quiz.prose: Some last digits stay the same for every power: $d, d^2, d^3, \ldots$ all end in $d$.
quiz.question: Which last digits behave this way? Select all that apply.

options.why: $4^2 = 16$ ends in 6. The powers of 4 alternate 4, 6.
$9^2 = 81$ ends in 1. The powers of 9 alternate 9, 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square each digit and see whether it returns.

explain.text: $0 \cdot 0$, $1 \cdot 1$, $5 \cdot 5 = 25$ and $6 \cdot 6 = 36$ keep their last digit. So every power does too, a cycle of length 1. Principle: test the edge case $d^2$ before hunting for a cycle.

quiz.question: What remainder does $2^{100}$ leave on division by 7?

byKey.four: 4 is $2^2$. The leftover power is 1, not 2.

explain.text: $2^{99} = (2^3)^{33}$ leaves 1, so $2^{100}$ leaves $2 \cdot 1 = 2$. Principle: find a power that leaves 1, then strip it off.

quiz.question: What is the last digit of the sum?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. From $5!$ on, every term ends in 0.

byKey.zero: Most terms end in 0, but $1! + 2! + 3! + 4!$ do not.
byKey.nine: You added 1, 2, 6 and 24 and slipped. The total is 33.

explain.text: From $5! = 120$ on, every term holds $2 \times 5$, so it ends in 0. The first four give $1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33$. The last digit is 3.
